E09.note: Inventory generated from the lockfile; the local check pipeline fails on a stale inventory or unreviewed licences.

O03.note: Self-hosted pipeline (lint, typecheck, unit, integration on PostgreSQL 16 and 18, licence and status checks, Chatwoot contract, accessibility, browser journeys) run with pnpm ci:local; --with-production also builds the images and checks the deployment. Every push to main can deploy itself without hosted CI. A signed GitHub webhook and a 5-minute check trigger it. The server checks and builds a clean copy of each version (Biome, type checks, unit tests, commit-tagged images), backs up before database changes, and starts the new version behind health checks and a soak period. Unhealthy versions are rolled back automatically. Changes a rollback cannot undo (destructive migrations, new versions of Chatwoot or PostgreSQL) wait for a deploy by hand, and migration mistakes stop the deploy. GitHub deployment statuses are reported when a token is set. All of this is tested end to end against a stand-in for GitHub.

W03.note: Each brand sets its main colour, logo, corner radius, greeting, offline text, rating on or off and privacy link in Studio, with a live picture of the chat in each language. The gateway refuses a colour whose text cannot be read or that fades into a white page (the same contrast check as the brand package) and Studio suggests a darker one. The widget draws itself from design tokens; a brand that changes nothing looks as before. Typography is not configurable, and the launcher position is a chat setting (W02).

HNV-24-06.note: Automated axe audits pass for every Storybook story in light/dark × LTR/RTL and for every Studio screen and dialog in English and Arabic, with no sideways scrolling from 320 to 1920 px (tested). Manual screen-reader, 200% zoom and keyboard reviews are still required.

D01.note: OpenAPI 3.1 from Zod (widget, identity, admin and developer routes: API keys, webhooks, allowed hosts, analytics, usage and invoices), RFC 9457 errors, Idempotency-Key replay/conflict, cursor pagination; servers authenticate with API keys. Remaining resources follow.

E04.note: Forward-compatible parsing and fixtures in place; client SDK compatibility tests follow with packages/client.

A09.note: Append-only, per-tenant hash-chained audit log (actor, action, target, outcome, reason, request ID, time and redacted data, with configuration versions where they apply) with filters, chain verification and CSV or NDJSON export behind its own permission and a fresh sign-in. The export is audited and never holds secrets or customer content. Studio filters the log, checks the chain and exports what it shows.

A06.note: Write-only, masked, envelope-encrypted secrets with rotation, revocation, KEK rotation and MFA + fresh sign-in. API keys for service accounts: scoped and expiring, shown once, stored as an HMAC, rotated with an overlap, revoked at once, rate-limited per key and audited. A workspace’s AI keys are replaced in place from Studio (the new key is stored, the old one revoked, agents carry on) and each can be tested with one tiny real call; Studio shows only yes or no for the keys the server holds.

O05.note: One-server production stack: gateway and edge images built from source, compose file with PostgreSQL 18 + pgvector, Valkey, Chatwoot 4.18.0-ce, ClamAV and Caddy (automatic HTTPS, HTTP to HTTPS, HTTP/3); only the edge publishes ports. hamnivo.sh sets up generated secrets and runs up, status, logs, backup, restore and update. The smoke test deploys it with Caddy's internal CA and checks sign-up, a real Chatwoot connection, an AI reply over the stream, the website and a backup and restore (tested). Studio is served at app.<domain> and used in a real browser by the smoke test. Let's Encrypt issuance needs public DNS and was not exercised here. Images are tagged and labelled with their commit, and the newest 3 versions are kept for rollback.

A02.note: Members are listed, invited (verified-email acceptance; resending replaces the link), given a role and scope in one step, suspended, restored and removed from Studio and the API, all within the delegation ceiling and audited. Suspension or removal ends workspace access on the next request and closes live streams at the next heartbeat; sign-in sessions end when no other workspace keeps the person. Privileged permissions need two-step verification and a fresh sign-in. Owner recovery is partial: the last owner cannot be removed, suspended or demoted, and owners recover their own account by verified email and backup codes, but nothing helps a workspace whose every owner has lost access.

A03.note: Delegation ceiling (own permissions, own scope, own expiry, no self-grants) enforced for grants, invitations and custom roles; interfaces added later (SCIM) must reuse checkDelegation.

X01.note: Staff principals come from server-verified sessions and per-request grant loading; service-account and workload identities pending.

X04.note: Secret broker reveals credentials only to server code inside the owning tenant; scoped short-lived credentials for tools and agents pending. MCP tokens, OAuth sign-ins (access and refresh tokens, client registrations) and the credentials of custom HTTP tools live in it and are never returned, logged or put in the audit log (tested); a credential replaced or removed is revoked.

O01.note: Prometheus metrics (request latency by route template, process metrics) behind a bearer token (tested: hidden without it, served with it) and liveness/readiness checks; alert rules and dashboards pending.

A11.note: A brand gets its Chatwoot account by itself: the first brand of a workspace (through the outbox, after a short wait) and a brand a billing system creates with its workspace (the tenant.created handler). Account, integration user with adoption guard, HMAC-mandatory API inbox with auto-assignment off, AI agent bot, signed webhooks and Copilot dashboard app; every step is recorded before the next (credentials with the secret broker), so a retry continues the same account, and Connect in Studio is the retry. Studio shows the set-up's progress or why it stopped (tested end to end against the fake, with failures and retries; provisioning also against real Chatwoot v4.18.0-ce). Channels (ADR 0013): email, WhatsApp and Telegram connect from Settings → Channels; discovery reads Chatwoot's reauthorization_required every few minutes and the card shows Needs attention with how to fix it (Fix sign-in for email). A channel still down after 15 minutes emails the people who manage the brand's integrations once, and once more when it works again (a delayed channel.health outbox event, handled once); the same people see a Studio banner linking to Channels. A shorter blip tells nobody. Tested end to end against the fake.

E06.note: One shared behaviour suite runs against every model provider (generate, stream, wire format, key placement, 401/429/5xx/529/abort) with provider-specific capability tests, and the Jev adapter has its own wire contract fixtures. Fixtures come from public API docs, not recorded traffic.

W05.note: History from Chatwoot's customer view (private notes and activity excluded) with earlier pages on request. Unread replies are counted from the customer's read point: a line where they start, a count on the launcher while the chat is closed (also in its accessible name) and a new-messages button with the count while reading back (tested in the gateway and the browser).

W06.note: Waiting for connection, sending, sent (only once the authority committed the message), read, and not sent with a readable reason and retry, edit and remove. Read only where Chatwoot reports it: its agent_last_seen_at, from webhooks or the reconciler, marks the customer's earlier messages read with one delivery.updated event. Chatwoot has no delivery receipts for this channel, so 'delivered' is not shown (tested in the gateway, the SDK and the browser).

W07.note: Resumable SSE (Last-Event-ID, backoff, idle watchdog, auth renewal, resync) and a persistent outbox that resends unsent messages with the same id after reloads or going offline. Drafts are kept per person and conversation across reloads and forgotten at sign-out. Server side, the worker's reconciler recovers messages and state changes whose Chatwoot webhooks were lost. All tested (unit, integration with every webhook dropped, and the browser).

W12.note: Anonymous start, ES256 access tokens, rotating refresh tokens with reuse revocation, and identity assertions signed by the tenant: kid, audience, a five-minute lifetime and a single-use jti. A new identity is a new principal: the old session and its streams end. Brands register their keys through the admin API, with two-step verification and a recent sign-in: ES256, EdDSA or RS256 public keys, or an HS256 secret shown once. Keys can be retired, or revoked, which also ends the chats they signed in. Assertions may be dated up to 5 seconds ahead. @hamnivo/server signs assertions. In the widget, identify shows the customer's own chats; reset clears the screen, ends the session in Hamnivo and in the browser, forgets unsent messages and clears other tabs; a late token renewal cannot undo either. All of this is tested, including in Chromium with a real key. The widget does not yet show the signed-in customer's name. Studio manages the keys too: create one (a shared secret is shown once, to copy), replace one (a new key of the same kind, the old one marked retiring) and revoke one.

H08.note: Atomic claim and takeover through the ownership epoch; an AI reply still being written when staff take over is fenced, and takeovers made inside Chatwoot are adopted (all tested). A reply from an out-of-date view (expected epoch) or over a colleague is refused and nothing is sent. Taking a conversation from a colleague needs conversations.assign; others ask for a transfer. Studio shows who else is viewing or typing, and ownership changes, live over the staff stream. Typing also goes between staff and the customer, as short-lived signals that are never stored, and each person’s online, away or offline status shows in the inbox.

R05.note: One public AI speaker per conversation fenced by the ownership epoch, and one AI reply per burst of customer messages: a reply is dropped when the customer wrote again meanwhile, and the newer message is answered with both in view (tested). The lease with expiry (columns present) is not used yet.

R06.note: Stale AI replies are rejected after takeover: at job start, at reservation under the row lock, by a Chatwoot pre-flight owner check and by a re-check of Hamnivo's own fence right before posting (each mutation-tested). A reply that still races a takeover while it is posted is marked late_publication, audited and reported to the new owner in a private note (tested). Undispatched tool actions follow with the tool gateway.

R12.note: 'Talk to a person' always moves the conversation to a durable waiting state with a private handoff note, and answers honestly: queued during business hours, offline with the return time outside them (tested); follow-up channels pending.

G02.note: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini and OpenAI-compatible adapters (AI SDK 7) plus deterministic mocks, a sourced capability table and error normalization; agents use them with tenant or platform keys, checked at publication, with fallback models on overload (tested against provider fixtures and with the mock end to end). No live provider call has run in the checks. A key can be tested with one minimal call (a few tokens, a 10 second limit, through the egress guard) and the failures are put in plain words: wrong key, no credit, model not found, network. That call is tested against provider fixtures only.

W01.note: One dependency-free script (1.7 KB gzip) adds an accessible launcher; the widget iframe is created only when opened (tested: nothing else loads before). In production the widget page carries CSP frame-ancestors from the brand's allowed websites (GET /v1/widget/frame-policy; tested through Caddy, including a spoofed header and an unknown widget). Brand colours from the published config are pending.

W04.note: Every message shows who wrote it with a text role label; AI answers carry the agent's configured display name from Hamnivo's record, never a Chatwoot-side name (tested).

W10.note: 'Talk to a person' in the widget creates a durable waiting state and a private handoff note for staff, so the customer does not repeat themselves (tested); context summary by AI pending.

W13.note: Language selector for English, Arabic, Hindi and Urdu with right-to-left layout for Arabic and Urdu (tested); translations pending native review.

W14.note: Keyboard operation (tested from the page's launcher into the chat's settings), Escape to close with focus returned to the launcher, labelled controls, polite live announcements, text size and less motion in the chat's settings with the device's own text size and reduced-motion setting applied first, reflow at 320 px and 200 % zoom, and axe audits with no WCAG 2.2 AA violations (tested). Manual screen-reader review pending.

D02.note: Framework-free SDK: sessions with single-flight renewal, typed conversation calls, exactly-once send outbox and resumable streams (unit-tested with msw, used by the widget).

D03.note: @hamnivo/react: a component that puts the chat on a React or Next.js page (marked use client; hidden when it unmounts; verifies the signed-in customer and signs the chat out with them), useHamnivo for the chat window, and hooks on @hamnivo/client for a custom chat (useHamnivoClient, useOutbox, useConversationStream). Tested in a real React against stand-ins for the loader and the API, and its Next.js snippets are type-checked. Not yet published to npm (a tag and the NPM_TOKEN secret do that), and not tried in a real app. The widget itself maps SDK state into assistant-ui's external-store runtime.

D04.note: @hamnivo/vue (plugin, component and composable for Vue 3 and Nuxt) and @hamnivo/react load the same loader and share one tested file for loading it; a tag-only workflow publishes either to npm. Tested in a real Vue against a stand-in for the loader; not yet published. They wrap the loader, not the headless client, and there is no Angular wrapper.

U04.note: Document direction follows the language; each message and the message box read in their own direction by letter majority, and Latin order numbers, amounts, emails and links are isolated left to right, also in Markdown answers. Copying gives back the exact text (browser-tested in Urdu with axe).

G01.note: Agents per brand with display name (a role, never a person), purpose, instructions, tone, reply languages, mode, model and limits; the brand's default agent answers its conversations (tested). Supported intents and a richer escalation policy pending.

G03.note: Answer mode replies to customers; assist mode writes suggestions only as internal notes and never answers customers (tested). Grounded answers from knowledge arrive with knowledge sources.

G09.note: Per-agent ceilings on output tokens, time, steps and history; model failures are retried twice by the outbox, then the conversation goes to people with an honest note (tested). Cost and concurrency budgets pending.

G12.note: Each run records agent version, provider, model, tokens, latency, outcome, error kind and per-step records; token usage goes to the usage ledger (tested). Cost estimates and dashboards pending.

X08.note: Kill switches for the tenant, a brand or an agent stop AI replies at once; AI-held conversations go to people on their next message, new conversations start with people, and clearing restores AI replies (tested, mutation-checked). Switches are cleared, never deleted. A tool switch stops one tool at once, including approvals already given (tested).

X11.note: Run and step records hold versions, counts, hashes and error kinds but no prompt or reply text (tested); staff read them through the API with analytics.read.

U09.note: Non-removable prompt rules plus an output guard for claims of being human in English, Hinglish, Roman Urdu, Hindi, Urdu and Arabic: regenerate once, otherwise publish nothing and hand over (tested, mutation-checked). Native-speaker review of the phrase lists pending.

A07.note: Saved drafts are not live; publishing freezes a version with its configuration hash (a database trigger rejects changes), one version is live at a time, and publishing an earlier version is the rollback (tested). Studio screens pending.

G04.note: Sources with owner, public/internal visibility, status and a review cycle; documents with versions, end dates, review and retirement; stale and expired documents stop grounding answers (tested). A website can be a source: its pages become documents, found through its sitemap and the links between them within one site and the folder of the address, with robots.txt followed, limits on pages and link depth, read on a schedule or on request. A changed page becomes a new version, and a page that is gone or now off limits is retired; a site that is down loses nothing (tested against a made-up site over real HTTP). The website panel in Studio is rendered in unit tests; there is no browser test of it.

G05.note: Hybrid vector + keyword retrieval with eligibility filters applied before ranking: tenant (RLS), brand, agent's sources, audience (internal sources never reach customer answers), current ready version, expiry and review cycle (tested). Per-customer document scopes pending.

G06.note: Answers cite retrieved passages; citation numbers that match nothing retrieved are removed and the rest renumbered per document; sources travel as source parts from Hamnivo's publication record and the widget lists them (tested). Before an AI reply is published, the answer check asks Jev, in one call, how each cited passage relates to each sentence that cites it (supports, contradicts or says nothing). Live: a reply with a sentence that is contradicted, unaddressed or below its threshold is never published; it is written again once without that sentence (within the run's time limit), then handed to people with a note. Shadow (every brand's start): recorded only. Jev unavailable or a language without thresholds: the reply goes out as before and the check is recorded; while the check is live, such replies are not cached and earlier cached answers are not reused. Verified live on 2026-10-02 with jev-1.13.0: a supported reply was published (231 ms) and a contradicted claim never reached the customer (147 ms, then 286 ms for the rewritten reply). No thresholds were evaluated for the answer check yet: each brand sets them per language. Replies are not streamed in this branch; the widget keeps any streamed draft provisional until it is published and drops it when it is withdrawn.

G17.note: Quarantined uploads, fail-closed scanning (ClamAV INSTREAM or the EICAR check), type sniffing, bounded parsing of text, Markdown, HTML, PDF and DOCX, sanitization, heading-aware chunking, embedding and indexing with progress states; the upload is cleared afterwards (tested). While the scanner is unreachable, uploads wait with backoff and are refused only after the last attempt (tested). Pages of a website enter the same pipeline: the crawler (one request at a time, every request through the egress guard, size and unpacking limits) hands over each page as an upload, in its own character set converted to UTF-8; a page whose text is built by JavaScript is left out (tested). Parsing runs in-process (no sandbox).

X09.note: Retrieved passages are fenced in the prompt as data with an explicit instruction to ignore instructions inside them, and staff messages are labelled; tool results reach the model fenced as untrusted data from a named tool, size-limited and checked, and a write proposed after reading another system’s data needs approval (tested). With the passage relevance check live, Jev also leaves out passages that carry instructions for the assistant (tested; verified live on one planted passage). Measuring injection resistance with an adversarial suite is X12. The answer of a custom HTTP tool is handled the same way (tested): fenced as data, size-limited, and a change proposed after reading it waits for a person.

W08.note: Agent and staff messages render Markdown through an allow-list sanitizer (no images, scripts or event handlers; http(s)/mailto links open in a new tab with noopener), and cited sources are listed under answers. Structured cards pending.

J01.note: Provider-neutral DecisionProvider port with a Jev adapter over the official @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 (pinned model, keyed maps) and a deterministic mock (tested with fixtures). Verified live on 2026-10-02 against jev-1.13.0: the opt-in adapter tests (`pnpm --filter @hamnivo/adapters test:live`, 5 of 5 passed) and 381 evaluation calls, all answered, p50 148 ms and p95 214 ms, about 673 input tokens per call, $0.0108 in all. Live tests are opt-in and never part of the default runs; the key is read from the environment only.

J04.note: A typed request for a person (English, Hinglish, Roman Urdu, Arabic, Hindi, Urdu, with negation and look-alikes) hands the conversation to people before any model or decision provider runs (tested end to end); For the rest, the escalation check asks Jev six questions about the customer's latest messages (personal data replaced by its kind), each one exact condition: asking for a person, frustrated or angry, a problem still not solved, a complaint, a legal threat, a risk to health or safety. Code combines them: a request, a safety risk, a legal threat or a complaint alone needs a person; frustration only together with an unsolved problem. Live: the conversation goes to people before any reply, with the reasons in the note; shadow (every brand's start): recorded only; Jev unavailable or a language without thresholds: the AI answers as today and the check is recorded. Jev can only add a hand-off, never block one. Verified live on 2026-10-02 with jev-1.13.0: a legal threat was handed over (139 ms) and a calm question went on to an answer (125 ms). Only the request for a person has evaluated thresholds (0.80, 0.90 for Roman Urdu); brands set the others from what shadow mode records. The message guard reads the same messages side by side: someone who says they want to hurt themselves, or that someone is in danger now, gets Hamnivo's safety wording at once in the reply language (no model writes it; it points to local emergency help), then people take over with an urgent note; a threat or abuse goes to people with the reason. The guard also reads every customer message while people have the conversation, and after the AI's early hand-offs (no agent, assist mode, kill switch; the wording is fixed text, so a kill switch does not hold it back): with nobody assigned, an urgent note and the wording go out at once; with a person assigned, the person gets the note with the words to send, and Hamnivo sends them after 2 minutes only if the AI does not have the conversation, Chatwoot shows no public reply since the customer's message and no wording went out in 24 hours. At most one wording per conversation in 24 hours and one urgent note per 10 minutes (tested). Shadow records only (tested; mutation-checked). Verified live on 2026-10-02 with jev-1.13.0: a message about ending one's life got the safety wording and was handed over (219 ms). Its thresholds were not evaluated: brands set them from what shadow mode records. Non-English safety wording is pending native review.

J06.note: Total deadline, caller cancellation (also when the transport ignores it), no retries, circuit breaker with half-open probe, and decided/abstained/unavailable/invalid results (tested). In the gateway, routing falls back to the deterministic baseline on abstained, unavailable or invalid results within the 1.5 s deadline (tested).

J07.note: Every decision result carries provider, model version, rubric version, answers, latency, token use and request id (tested). Routing decisions are persisted as decision records (status, confidence only when given, latency, tokens, shadow or live, policy version) and shown in Studio; cost is kept as tokens. Checks around AI replies are recorded in decision_checks (written once; labels, numbers and document ids, never text) with the same versions, latency and tokens, and as steps of the run.

E08.note: Requests and answers use the current keyed-map shapes, checked against an exact fixture; array-shaped answers from the older client are rejected. Proven against the SDK and fixtures, not the live API.

U02.note: Hinglish and Roman Urdu requests for a person are detected across spellings (banday, bande, banda, insaan, insan, aadmi, admi, real person), transliterations and negation, including "... ki zaroorat nahi" (101 fixture cases), and act end to end; identifiers pass through unchanged. Native-speaker review pending.

O02.note: hamnivo.sh backup dumps both databases (pg_dump), Chatwoot files, certificates and settings with checksums and keeps the newest N. Restore checks the checksums and refuses a backup made with other secrets. It restores the Hamnivo database beside the current one, runs pending migrations and adds the memory consent, deletion receipts and tombstones made since the backup, replaying the tombstones. Only then does it swap databases, so a failed restore leaves the current one as it was. The production smoke test runs a drill (tested): a brand made after the backup is gone, and the conversation history is back. A consent withdrawn and a customer's memory erased after the backup both stay that way. Point-in-time recovery and off-site copies are pending.

X13.note: Replaying a whole conversation through the reconciler neither duplicates messages nor repeats a takeover, and repeated webhook deliveries are applied once (tested). Commerce: replayed payment and refund webhooks, repeated approval taps, lost provider answers (timeouts before and after the provider acted) and repeated worker runs leave one payment page, one charge, one refund and one card each (tested). Pending: tool crash cases, and a test that kills the worker process mid-call.

W15.note: Customers rate a resolved conversation (1 to 5 with an optional comment) and reopen it with I still need help, from the rating card or, when rating is off, from the closed banner; staff see each rating as a private note, and a reopened AI conversation returns to people if the AI may no longer answer (tested in the gateway and the browser).

W11.note: Brands set business hours, and the widget says honestly who can answer: online, here but busy, away until a time in the brand's time zone, or nobody online. When the hours are closed or nobody is online (the brand chooses), a contact form takes the customer's message: it becomes a ticket for people (H19), and one email asks to confirm the address without repeating what was written; answers are emailed only to a confirmed address. Offline, the widget keeps unsent messages and sends them once. Tested in the gateway (20 cases) and in the browser, including Arabic at 320 px. Replying by email waits for the email channel (D13).

A04.note: Each brand has its own widget ID, allowed websites and business hours. Studio creates and edits brands; a website taken off the list gets no frame permission (CSP frame-ancestors per brand), no new chats, and its open chats end at once (tested). Per-brand appearance editing (board 04) is next.

HNV-02-01.note: Email and password with password-manager-friendly fields, single sign-on by work email (with SSO required, passwords and passkeys turn to SSO), passkeys, and recovery through a verified email, all tested end to end. The workspace is chosen after sign-in rather than shown on the sign-in page.

HNV-02-03.note: Authenticator-app codes with a backup-code option; tested end to end: turn it on, sign out, sign in with a code.

HNV-02-05.note: Sensitive actions and ended sessions ask to sign in again over the page; unsaved work is kept and the action finishes afterwards (tested). A password with a code, a passkey or single sign-on confirm it; people who use SSO are offered it first, and the provider is asked to check who they are again (prompt=login).

HNV-02-06.note: Pages a person may not open say what access is missing and who can grant it.

HNV-03-02.note: A new workspace’s overview says what to do first: a Get set up list with the steps still open (connect the chat engine, add a brand and install the chat, publish an AI agent, invite a teammate), each linking to its page and gone once all are done; people who do not run the workspace see their chats instead (tested). The test widget comes later.

HNV-03-05.note: A Search button in the header and ⌘K or Ctrl+K anywhere (by the physical key, so Arabic, Hindi and Urdu keyboard layouts work) open every page the person can open, grouped as the menu is: the menu's pages, plus the pages behind buttons (guided setup, live visitors, saved replies and tags, blocked visitors, Stop AI) only for people those buttons are shown to, and the account pages. Typing narrows by the page's name, its group's name or its English name; every typed word must appear, so scattered letters never match. The arrow keys choose, Enter opens the page with focus on its heading, Esc closes with focus back where it was, and the shortcut does not open over another dialog. Tested in unit and jsdom tests (mutation-checked) and in Chromium, in English at desktop width and in Arabic at 390 px, with no axe WCAG 2.2 AA violations. Recent pages and actions other than opening a page are not offered.

HNV-11-02.note: Agent drafts are edited and saved by keyboard alone, and a draft someone else changed is shown as a conflict instead of being overwritten (tested).

HNV-11-06.note: Publishing asks for a fresh sign-in and then shows the live version (tested); rollback in Studio comes later.

HNV-13-06.note: Stopping AI replies for a brand shows the scope first, is visible everywhere afterwards and can be undone (tested).

HNV-14-01.note: The knowledge library lists sources with their status (tested); a website says so under its name with how its reading stands (unit-tested).

HNV-14-02.note: An uploaded file shows its progress until it is ready to search (tested); a website shows that it is waiting or being read, how its last read went and each page’s state (unit-tested, no browser test); cancelling an import comes later.

HNV-14-04.note: Search preview shows the passages an answer could cite (tested).

HNV-17-02.note: Connecting Chatwoot says what will be created, in which account, before anything happens (tested).

HNV-17-03.note: A connected brand shows its connection status and Chatwoot account (tested); capabilities and last sync come later.

HNV-17-05.note: Each brand shows a copyable install snippet, and its allowed websites can be changed (tested); an event test comes later.

D05.note: One-click installs for four platforms, with a guide for each: a WordPress plugin (settings page, Test connection, verified customers for WordPress users and WooCommerce customers; tested in a real WordPress and WooCommerce on PHP 7.4 to 8.5), a WHMCS addon (loader, verified clients, optional product names; tested with stand-ins for WHMCS on PHP 7.4 to 8.5), a Shopify app embed (rendered with LiquidJS, and Shopify's Theme Check finds no offenses), and a Google Tag Manager template (run in a stand-in for its sandbox). All sign with a PHP SDK that matches @hamnivo/server byte for byte against its fixtures. pnpm build:integrations writes the zips and the template. Nothing is tried in a real WHMCS, Shopify store or Tag Manager yet, and the Shopify app and the Gallery listing need the owner's Partner and Google accounts.

L01.note: Memory records use the typed envelope (kind, scope, source, evidence status, purposes, roles, sensitivity, retention, policy version) and a closed catalogue of slots; the write policy sets every governing field and claims stay unverified (tested). Only preference, observation and claim slots exist so far; procedure, commitment and outcome kinds have no slots yet.

L02.note: Records are bound to tenant (RLS), brand and customer principal, with source messages, conversation, writer and write reason; reads check the customer, brand, purpose and role, and staff actions are authorized per brand with memory.read, manage, delete, erase and export and audited without content (tested, including other customers of the same brand, other tenants and staff without permission).

L03.note: Corrections supersede and never overwrite: content is immutable (enforced by a trigger), each record has event and transaction time, one current value per slot, and older words cannot reopen a slot that changed since. A disagreeing value waits for review and neither is used until the customer or staff confirm; the history stays inspectable (tested).

L04.note: Customers agree or decline, see what is remembered with its source and expiry, correct, confirm, delete, forget everything and turn memory off in the widget; staff do the same in Studio within their grants (tested in the API and in browsers, including right to left). Retention is fixed per memory type; letting brands or customers configure it is pending. Staff also see, correct and delete a customer’s memory beside the conversation in the inbox (unit-tested, no browser test).

L05.note: A deletion removes records, their vectors and memory citations in answers and the realtime journal, and leaves content-free tombstones (keyed fingerprints). Its receipt completes only after caches are purged and nothing covered is left; retention expiry uses the same path. Replayed jobs and restored rows cannot bring memory back: the write policy and a database trigger refuse them, recall skips them and the tombstones are replayed daily (tested). A restore carries over the receipts, tombstones and consent made after the backup from the current database and replays them before anything starts; deletions still running are queued again (tested in the production drill). Pending: learning datasets do not exist yet. A restore on a new server has no current database, so deletions made after its backup are lost with the old server.

L07.note: The model only proposes from the message that started the job; a pure, deterministic policy decides with an explanation that contains no content. It checks consent and its timing, the slot catalogue, sensitive categories (health, religion, ethnicity, sexual orientation, political views) and secrets (passwords, codes, card and account numbers) in English, Roman Urdu, Urdu, Hindi and Arabic, authority claims and instructions, provenance (quote must be in the customer message), confidence, identity for personal details, retention, tombstones and per-customer limits (tested, with mutation checks).

K09.note: Memory is never put in a shared cache: memory is recalled before the answer cache is read, a reply built with any memory item carries personal_memory and shared entries refuse it, and memory endpoints send no-store. Per-customer answer entries live in the customer's memory namespace and are keyed by their memory version, so a memory change makes them unreachable and a deletion purges them (tested end to end with a correction and a deletion, mutation-checked). A scope that is missing, slow or not the customer's own means nothing is cached for them. Pending: cached values are stored unencrypted in Valkey.

G19.note: Replies use only consented, current, in-scope memory of the conversation's own customer that allows AI use and is not under review, ranked by vectors and words within the agent's budget and fenced as data. Answers cite them as memories ([M1] becomes a memory part the widget shows as “based on what you told us before”), never as something said in the chat; turning memory off, outdated, expired and future values are never used (tested).

HNV-15-01.note: The chat asks before remembering anything: what, why, what is never kept and for how long, with two equal answers and nothing preselected (tested with an accessibility audit, also in Urdu and Arabic). Translations await native review.

HNV-15-02.note: Studio lists customers with memory and shows each memory with purpose, source message, who recorded it, scope, expiry and history; customers see theirs in the widget (tested, including right to left). The inbox panel lists each memory with its source and the day it was observed.

HNV-15-03.note: A newer, different value waits for review: Studio compares both and confirms the new one or keeps the current one with a reason (tested); the customer is asked to confirm it in the widget (tested).

HNV-15-04.note: Corrections by staff (with a reason) and by customers replace the value and keep the old one in the history (tested).

HNV-15-05.note: Deleting says what is removed and what stays (audit record, chat history), then shows progress until indexes and caches are cleared; erasing a customer works the same way (tested).

HNV-15-06.note: Staff without memory.read see an access-denied state and no navigation entry (tested); the widget says when memory is unavailable and the chat keeps working (tested).

H01.note: Queues for mine, waiting for a person, AI answering, my teams and all, with counts, keyset paging and filters by status (open or pending, snoozed, resolved), brand, channel, customer language and tag. Lists, counts, search and the staff stream all apply the same grant filter (workspace, brand, inbox or team): a conversation outside a person's grants is not found. Tested through the API and in the browser. Each person sees which chats have news for them: unread is kept by the server per person, not per browser, and shows in the list, the page title and the tab icon, with sounds and desktop alerts that are theirs to set (tested).

H02.note: Manual routing: claim, assign to a colleague who may reply there, back to the queue, back to the AI, and team queues (teams belong to Hamnivo and are mirrored to Chatwoot with their members). Every owner change goes through the ownership epoch and is audited. Round-robin and capacity checks are not built yet. Studio lists the teams and adds or takes out people (the Support teams page).

H03.note: Internal notes are Chatwoot private notes written as the staff member. They never reach the customer's stream or history, or the AI's prompt (tested through the API and through the widget in the browser). Studio shows them with a lock, a text label and a dashed border, and writes them in a separate composer lane.

H04.note: Only tags defined for the brand (Chatwoot labels) are accepted, and custom fields are checked against their definitions (text, number, list, date, link, checkbox); Chatwoot's other attributes are kept. Tags are copied into Hamnivo for queue filters. People who manage the inbox add, rename, recolour and delete tags in Studio (Saved replies and tags, inbox.manage on the brand): a rename or a delete reaches the conversations in Chatwoot and in Hamnivo’s copy, open inboxes are told, and each change is audited. Tag names follow Chatwoot’s own rule (two characters or more, letters and numbers, no vowel signs). The Chatwoot calls are covered by the fake and by contract cases whose run against a real Chatwoot is left to CI. New custom fields are still defined in Chatwoot.

H05.note: Chatwoot canned responses, searched as the staff member, with variables filled from verified facts only (an address nobody verified is never filled in) and missing variables listed. People who manage the inbox add, edit and delete saved replies in Studio (Saved replies and tags): each short code is used once, a detail such as the customer’s first name is added with a button, the composer sees every change at once, and each change is audited without the text of the reply. The contract cases against a real Chatwoot are left to CI.

H06.note: Verified or anonymous identity and what that means, a verified email apart from an address nobody verified, language, brand, Chatwoot contact attributes (Hamnivo's internal ones left out) and the other conversations the person can see. A third column on wide screens, a sheet otherwise. A Website visit card shows the customer’s current page, the pages seen, device, country and number of visits. Browsers that send Do Not Track are left out, no IP address is stored, page addresses lose their query string unless the brand chooses otherwise, and everything is deleted 30 days after the visitor was last seen (tested). Beside the customer, the panel shows what the AI remembers about them, each memory with its source, for people who may read memory in the brand; people with the right grants correct or delete a memory there (tested in the gateway and in unit tests; no browser test).

H07.note: Customers by name, email or conversation ID in Hamnivo, and message text (notes included) in Chatwoot as the staff member, in pages. Hits outside the person's grants are dropped, and Chatwoot accounts they cannot reach are not searched.

H09.note: Personal drafts per conversation and lane, with revisions: a save from an older revision is refused and shown as a choice. A copy stays in the browser while offline and is saved when the connection is back. A failed send is kept with its reason, and retrying it with the same message ID never posts twice (tested with a Chatwoot timeout after the message was stored).

H10.note: Resolve, reopen and snooze (an hour, until tomorrow, until next week or a chosen time) in Chatwoot as the staff member; each change is audited and shown to the customer. Reopening makes the person the owner, as Chatwoot does.

H11.note: Suggested replies from the brand's agent with the knowledge it cited, built from customer-visible messages only, recorded as a draft run and never sent on their own. Copy, edit, or Send as me through the ownership-checked send (audited). Conversation summaries and next-step suggestions are not built yet.

H13.note: A customer message can be translated into the staff member's language on demand through the brand's model, labelled as a machine translation under the unchanged original; the model is told to keep names, numbers and identifiers. Writing a reply in the customer's language is not built yet.

H14.note: Supervisors (conversations.review) rate a conversation and leave a coaching note about its owner. Taking over from a colleague is limited to people with conversations.assign; anyone else can ask for a transfer, which reaches the owner as an internal note.

H15.note: Assign, team, status and tag changes for up to 50 conversations. A dry run says which ones the change would reach, each conversation is checked like a single change, and failures are listed with their reason and can be retried alone. There is no undo.

H17.note: Conversations can be linked, with a note, and unlinked; both keep their own authors, times, notes and sources. Merging and splitting are left out on purpose: Chatwoot keeps the transcripts.

HNV-07-05.note: Staff inbox: machine translation labelled, under the original, with hide and show; a failed translation leaves the original as it was.

HNV-07-06.note: Staff inbox on a phone: queue, conversation and details as steps; the details sheet has a visible close button, Esc closes it and focus returns; Back returns to the row.

HNV-08-02.note: Atomic claim that shows the owner when someone else claimed first; the SLA status waits for H12.

HNV-09-05.note: On-demand suggestions with their sources, edit, dismiss or send as me. Drafts that an assist-mode agent prepares on its own are not shown yet.

HNV-10-03.note: Hamnivo's handoff summary (why, the customer's words and language, completed and pending actions, facts with their sources) is shown to staff as a staff-only card and in the inbox and the conversation can be claimed; rejecting with a capacity reason is not built yet.

C01.note: Each brand has at most one active merchant connection (Stripe, or the mock provider outside production) with currencies, delivery, refund policy and a capability manifest. The API key and webhook secret are stored only in the secret broker: responses show them masked, and they never reach logs, audit data or the browser. Connecting and rotating keys need two-step verification and are audited (tested). Connections are managed through the API; a Studio screen is pending.

E02.note: Each connection publishes a versioned capability manifest (catalog, hosted checkout, full and partial refunds, currencies, recurring, provisioning). Operations are checked against it before any provider call. An unsupported checkout is refused with a plain reason and the cart is kept; when the provider refunds only whole payments, Studio offers the full amount (tested).

C02.note: Product cards come from the merchant's live catalog (Stripe prices are the variants). They show the seller, the price with its currency, stock as the merchant reports it, and when it was read; a snapshot keeps what was shown. Products are listed side by side; there is no separate comparison view. Recurring products are left out until C14 (tested).

C03.note: Carts are versioned, and a stale revision is refused. Quotes are priced live by the provider in exact integer minor units (lines, discount, delivery, tax, total), checked again before they are saved, and expire. Approval binds to the canonical hash of the quote document (RFC 8785, SHA-256) (tested).

C04.note: The approval card shows the seller, lines, delivery, total, refund terms, expiry, and that payment happens on the provider's page. The widget recomputes the quote hash before it enables Approve, and the server accepts only that hash and cart revision, once. A changed cart invalidates the approval, an expired quote cannot be approved, and the button is disabled at expiry (tested).

C05.note: Payment happens on Stripe Checkout (hosted page, opened in a new tab); the chat never collects card details. The model's context holds the conversation and card summaries but no payment page link, session or payment reference (tested). The Stripe adapter is tested against stripe-mock (when STRIPE_MOCK_URL is set) and a stateful fake; it has not been run against Stripe's live test mode.

C06.note: When the bank asks the customer to confirm a payment (3-D Secure), the purchase stays on the same open payment page. The chat says so, another tap cannot start a second purchase, and paying there completes it once; a repeated challenge event changes nothing (tested with the mock provider and, in the browser, the fake Stripe). Not yet checked against Stripe's live test mode.

C07.note: Every checkout and refund call is an operation with a durable business key (unique per tenant) and one provider idempotency key. The exact request is stored, so a resend is identical, and every observation is an append-only receipt. A lost request is resent under the same key only inside the provider's key window; after that it is looked up by its reference, never sent again, and a person is asked (tested).

C08.note: Webhooks are verified with the Stripe SDK's constructEvent over the raw body, using the connection's secret from the broker, and checked against the connection's account. Each is stored once per provider event id, then applied by the worker through the state machines. Replayed deliveries are applied once; tampered, stale and foreign-secret ones are refused (tested). Not yet received from Stripe's live test mode.

C09.note: A timeout after the provider acted leaves the purchase unknown: never failed, never sent again blindly. The worker finds the session by its reference and continues, so the purchase ends paid with one charge. A lost webhook is found by asking the provider (tested with the mock provider and the fake Stripe; not yet against the live test mode).

C10.note: An order is created with the payment page and confirmed only by a captured payment. Fulfilment is separate: staff record in progress, delayed (with the shop's estimate), shipped, delivered, active or failed. Paid, shipped and delivered stay distinct for staff and customers, and each step is posted to the chat (tested). Updates are entered by staff; reading them from the merchant's system is pending (see C18).

C12.note: A refund is checked for eligibility (captured payment, amount left, window, provider capability) and the merchant's approval policy. The person who asked can never approve it, approving needs two-step verification, and it shows as refunded only after the provider confirms it. A lost answer is found instead of refunding twice (tested with the mock provider and the fake Stripe; not yet against the live test mode).

C18.note: P1, not started in this wave: the P0 commerce work came first. Service fulfilment is recorded by staff for now (C10).

C19.note: Unknown and failed payments and refunds, amount mismatches and orders that could not be updated open a finance exception with its evidence and the next safe action. Finance can check with the provider, or resolve with a reason; resolving is audited and moves no money (tested).

C20.note: The commerce suite checks the final financial state after duplicate taps and webhooks, timeouts before and after the provider acted, lost requests outside the provider's key window, stale and expired quotes, a price change after the quote, a cancel after payment, a bank challenge, a takeover with a payment in flight, and cross-tenant access (gateway integration and browser tests; the key checks were mutation-tested).

R07.note: Operations keep their conversation and the ownership epoch they started in. Whenever a person becomes the owner (a takeover, an inbox claim, a supervisor's assignment, an assignment or reply in Chatwoot), a private note lists the payments and refunds still owed an outcome and asks them not to repeat them; a move back to the queue waits for the next person. The worker keeps reconciling whoever owns the conversation, and the conversation's commerce view lists what is in flight (tested for the takeover, the inbox claim and an assignment).

X10.note: A payment or refund counts as done only with a succeeded receipt from the provider. An AI reply that claims one without it is regenerated once with a correction, then the conversation goes to people; an open payment page is not a payment (tested). Replies about changes AI actions made have the same check (G14). After the receipt check, which runs first and keeps the final say, the message guard asks Jev whether a draft says or promises a payment, refund or order change, in any wording or language. Each is held against Hamnivo's records, never the text: a payment or refund needs its receipt, a promised refund one submitted to the provider, and an order change the succeeded receipt of an AI action in the conversation, in the same operation ledger (a promised one, an action approved or sent; a lookup backs none). Live: the draft is written again once with a correction, then people take over with a note; a reply that states one is never cached; shadow records only (tested; mutation-checked). Verified live on 2026-10-02 with jev-1.13.0: a draft that cancelled an order and promised a refund was held back (121 ms) and the rewrite went out (166 ms). Thresholds not evaluated yet.

U06.note: Amounts are exact minor units formatted for the locale with the currency always shown; times always carry their zone, and shop dates (delivery estimates) are shown as calendar dates. Typed amounts in Latin, Arabic-Indic, Persian and Devanagari digits are read exactly, and an ambiguous one such as "1,500" is asked, not guessed (tested). Pending: native-language review of the wording and number display.

U15.note: Quote cards name the seller and show every line, delivery, tax, the total, the refund terms, how long the price holds, and that payment happens on the provider's page. Stock is shown only as the merchant reports it, with no urgency messages. Recurring products are not sold in chat until C14 (tested in English and Arabic). The Arabic, Hindi and Urdu text awaits native review.

E12.note: The commerce module owns the purchase, payment, order and refund lifecycles through explicit state machines, and the AI has no commerce tools. Prices come only from live provider quotes, only the signed-in customer approves their quote, only staff with the right permission request or approve refunds, and the AI may state an outcome only with a receipt (tested).

K06.note: Every commerce response is sent with Cache-Control: no-store, prices and stock are read live for each quote (a catalog snapshot is never used to charge), and answerCacheDecision() decides for the answer cache: commerce registers it as a cache exclusion rule in both processes, so a reply in a conversation that holds catalog, cart, quote, payment, order or refund data is neither read from nor written to the cache, and a reply whose receipt check read a payment or refund status is not stored. Tested end to end with a paid order next to a plain knowledge answer that is still cached, and mutation-checked.

HNV-20-01.note: Live product cards with price, currency, stock as reported and when it was read (tested in the browser with axe).

HNV-20-02.note: Quantity controls change a draft cart only; nothing is bought until a quote is approved. Delivery and tax appear in the exact quote; the address is collected on the provider's payment page (tested).

HNV-20-03.note: Seller, lines, delivery, total, refund terms, expiry and cancel. A changed cart or an expired price returns to review (tested in English and Arabic, with axe).

HNV-20-04.note: The provider's page opens in a new tab with the order reference; no card fields in the chat; cancelling returns to the kept cart; after a bank challenge the same page finishes the payment (tested).

HNV-20-05.note: Coming back from the page shows 'confirming', never 'paid', until the provider's event; Check status asks the provider without starting a second payment (tested).

HNV-20-06.note: A cancelled, expired or refused payment page says nothing was charged and keeps the cart for a fresh quote; nothing is bought again automatically (tested).

HNV-21-01.note: A receipt card with the order reference appears only after the provider confirms the payment; fulfilment is shown separately (tested).

HNV-21-02.note: Staff record a delay in Studio with the shop's estimate. The chat shows the milestone, the estimate as an estimate (not a promise), when it was updated, and Talk to a person (tested in both, with axe; Studio also in Urdu).

HNV-21-03.note: Cancellation and returns are C11 (wave A).

HNV-21-04.note: Amount, reason, policy and approver. The requester cannot approve their own refund; approval needs two-step verification; rejection needs a reason (tested, with axe and in Arabic).

HNV-21-05.note: Refund reference, amount, the provider's state, last update and Check status. A refund is never shown as refunded before the provider confirms it, and a failed one opens a finance exception (tested).

J02.note: Routing runs on the first customer message and on every hand-off. Brands start in shadow mode: Jev and the deterministic baseline are both recorded and only the baseline is applied (no team assignment from Jev). Live mode applies Jev when it is sure enough per language, otherwise the baseline, within a 1.5 s deadline behind the circuit breaker. Explicit requests for a person are never overridden. Routing chooses among the inbox's teams with active, accepting routing for the brand and applies the choice the inbox's way: the conversation joins the team's queue and the inbox sync sets the Chatwoot team; a team a person chose, or a person handling the conversation, is kept. Behaviour is tested against a fake Jev and the fake Chatwoot. Verified live on 2026-10-02 with jev-1.13.0: through the gateway (`pnpm --filter @hamnivo/gateway test:live`), Studio's test panel and a shadow conversation routed 6 of 6 messages in English, Arabic, Hindi, Urdu and Roman Urdu to the right team, 135 to 233 ms each; on 266 labelled messages Jev chose the right topic for 260 (97.7%), the fixed keyword rule for 188 (70.7%). The evaluated default threshold is 0.50 in every language; Studio fills it in when Jev is chosen.

J05.note: Versioned rubric per brand (draft, publish), pinned Jev version, deadline, topics with baseline keywords, inputs shared with Jev (personal data redacted) and a threshold per language slice (no threshold means Jev abstains there). Studio editor with server validation on the fields, publish confirmation and a test panel. Arabic, Hindi and Urdu text is pending native review. Reply checks have the same versioned rubrics (provider, pinned version, deadline, thresholds per language and question) and shadow or live mode per brand, in Studio's Reply checks page.

J08.note: Jev versus baseline from shadow and live records: agreement, accuracy against human reviews, abstained, unavailable and invalid counts, latency p50/p95 and tokens, overall and per language. Offline, `run-suite decisions --provider jev` compares Jev with the fixed rules per language on labelled messages: accuracy, Brier score, calibration error, abstention at thresholds, latency and cost at $0.042 per million input tokens, capped at 2,000 calls. Run live on 2026-10-02 (381 calls): routing 97.7% against 70.7% for the fixed rule, language 86.8% against 70.0%, request for a person 98.7% (the fixed rule, which always decides first, 100% on its own test cases), p50 148 ms, p95 214 ms, $0.0000283 per decision; the default thresholds come from this run. Studio's experiment view still shows tokens, not money.

U01.note: Interface locale, explicit reply language (BCP 47, including hi-Latn and ur-Latn), detected language with an ask-once rule for Hinglish/Roman Urdu ambiguity, and style are kept separately per customer; replies follow the explicit choice, then the words, then the locale. Hinglish and Roman Urdu are never treated as English. Messages are not stored. Timezone is not part of the model yet. When the words fit more than one language and the customer has not chosen, the language check asks Jev the evaluated language question; its thresholds are by the language Jev answered (measured live: 0.50 for English, Arabic, Hindi and Urdu, 0.55 for Roman Urdu, none for Hinglish). Live: a sure enough answer settles the language and the customer is not asked; otherwise the customer is asked once, as before; shadow (every brand's start) only records. The customer's own choice always wins, and Jev is not asked then (tested). Verified live on 2026-10-02 with jev-1.13.0: for "order abhi tak nahi aaya, kab aayega?" Jev answered Hinglish, which has no threshold, so the customer was asked (254 ms).

HNV-07-04.note: The widget asks once which language replies should use when the words fit Hinglish and Roman Urdu (suggestion from the interface locale first); the choice or "not now" is saved on the server and the message stays as sent. Browser-tested in Urdu with axe. Arabic, Hindi and Urdu text is pending native review.

U05.note: Key-coverage tests for the widget and Studio: every key in all four locales, the same placeholders, no empty or copied English text. New screens are complete in all four locales. Server validation messages, emails and receipts are not localized yet. Arabic, Hindi and Urdu text is pending native review.

U07.note: Teams are the inbox's teams. Per brand, a team's routing lists the languages it answers in and those it serves through a reviewed translation path, with its topics and whether it is the default or accepting; a team routes only for brands of its own workspace (enforced in the database). Routing prefers a team that speaks the customer's language, then a translation path, then a language gap (recorded as the language match), and treats Hinglish and Roman Urdu as alternatives when the words fit both. Staff can be ranked by language the same way. Studio edits a team's routing per brand.

U08.note: Enter sends and Shift+Enter adds a line; an Enter that confirms an input method composition never sends (isComposing, composition events and Safari's key code 229). The box and each message read in their own direction by letter majority; order numbers, amounts, emails and links are isolated left to right, also in Markdown answers, and copy back unchanged. Browser-tested with axe in Urdu; the tests were mutation-checked.

U10.note: Style (concise, conversational or formal; gentle or direct) is stored per customer and turned into prompt lines that change wording only. There is no widget control yet and facts-preserved-across-styles is not evaluated yet.

U11.note: Non-removable reply rules: correct false assumptions politely with what the information shows, admit uncertainty and earlier errors, never agree to be agreeable. The same rules drive the offline evaluation; results with a real model are pending.

U12.note: Offline harness, starter corpus (12 scenarios in six language slices, each neutral and under five kinds of pressure), metrics with Wilson intervals and a CLI. CI runs a subset with a faithful and a sycophantic reference (the second is caught) and the mock model. Results with a real model and native review of the corpus are pending.

U13.note: Fairness groups swap names, gender markers, politeness, script and language and check the product's own routing baseline, hand-off detection and personal data check; every swap is gated at 100% in CI and any variant that gets a different decision is listed as a finding. The Roman Urdu request for a person with "banday" that the pairs found is now detected. Reply-level pairs with a model and native review are pending.

U14.note: Six scenarios in six slices: the product's reply language choice and the stated facts are checked automatically, and review packets (JSON plus a sheet per slice) wait for native speakers; meaning and tone rates come only from their reviews. All packets are pending native review.

K01.note: Exact answer cache, off until a brand turns it on. Only a first, public, complete answer without personal data, personal context or excluded classes is stored in shared entries; keys bind tenant, brand, audience, language, model, prompt version, every dependency version and a per-tenant HMAC of the question, and hits are rechecked against the current knowledge. A reply built with customer memory never enters a shared entry: it is kept for that customer alone, in their memory namespace and keyed by their memory version. Never crosses tenants, brands or customers (tested, mutation-checked). The index keeps fingerprints and references only.

K02.note: Query embeddings for knowledge search are cached under the exact text, the embedding model, its dimensions and the preprocessing version; queries with personal data are not cached.

K07.note: Database triggers bump dependency versions in the same transaction as knowledge, source, agent and brand changes; policy changes and manual invalidation bump the tier. Old keys stop being read at once, stale entries are reported, and cleanup of stored copies reports failures separately.

K08.note: A store that fails or times out (150 ms) reads as unavailable, is skipped for 30 s and answers are computed fresh; human messaging never waits on the cache (tested with a hanging store). Concurrent misses are coalesced per process for embeddings; answers are not coalesced yet.

K10.note: Daily counts per brand, tier and language: hits, misses, bypasses, stale, stores, errors, saved tokens, saved time and lookup time, with no content; store health from a live probe. False hits are counted only as rechecks that failed; cost in money is not computed.

K12.note: One small store interface with Valkey (prefixed, dedicated connection, short timeouts) and bounded in-memory implementations, a fail-open wrapper and singleflight; policy stays in the domain.

HNV-12-01.note: Rubric draft with topics, allowed outputs (plus "other"), inputs and per-language thresholds; malformed keys and unpinned Jev versions are refused before anything goes live. Arabic, Hindi and Urdu text is pending native review.

HNV-12-02.note: The test panel shows the typed result, the policy interpretation (explicit request, redacted inputs), the topic and team used and the request id; it can be run again with another message.

HNV-12-03.note: Abstention is labelled as "not sure"; the baseline decides and no confidence is shown unless the provider gave one.

HNV-12-04.note: An answer that fails the contract is recorded as invalid with a diagnostic reason for administrators and never enters business state; the baseline decides.

HNV-12-05.note: A deadline or open circuit is recorded as unavailable and the baseline route continues at once; requests for a person are never blocked.

HNV-12-06.note: Reviewers record the correct topic, a reason and a separate consent to use the label in evaluations; reviews are audited and feed the comparison.

HNV-25-01.note: Tiers with their time to keep, versioned per brand; personal, identity, account, memory, live order, payment, approval and tool data are never cached whatever the settings. Arabic, Hindi and Urdu text is pending native review.

HNV-25-02.note: The inspector shows tier, fingerprint, knowledge versions, language, a preview of the public answer and the expiry, without counting or changing anything.

HNV-25-03.note: A miss says why (not stored yet, or out of date) and the answer is computed fresh; admission happens only for complete, still eligible answers.

HNV-25-04.note: Personal data, later turns, personal context and excluded requests (the commerce hook) bypass with a reason code; nothing of them is stored or logged.

HNV-25-05.note: Invalidation shows the affected entries, stops reads at once by bumping versions, marks entries no longer used and reports copies that could not be removed yet.

HNV-25-06.note: When the store is down, answers are computed fresh and Studio shows the degraded state, recent failures and the error counts; a tier can be turned off from the policy.

M01.note: Before anything is imported, an export is scanned and read: counts, the fields found with how each is imported, required fields, known limits of the source and every record that needs review, with the destination checked (Chatwoot connected, a quiet import inbox, no automation or integration acting on imports, the importer’s permissions) and a file from another source refused (tested, also in browsers).

M02.note: The Hamnivo package: NDJSON records (or a ZIP with a manifest, checksums and an attachments manifest), a JSON Schema generated from the model, raw source references, and export of a brand’s history in the same format, read back by the importer (round trip tested).

M03.note: tawk.to JSON exports (ZIP or JSON) import end to end, with the 50-chat export cap, cut-short chats and file links reported (tested with fixtures shaped on tawk.to’s documented export; not yet checked against a real export). Importing through the tawk.to REST API is not built: it needs tawk.to’s approval.

M04.note: Another Chatwoot account is read with a user’s access token kept only in the secret broker and revoked after one read: paginated conversations and messages with their contacts and files, oldest first, a set number per import with later imports continuing; the address must be public https (checked again on every connection). Tested against the fake and, for the read path, against Chatwoot 4.18.

M05.note: Separate connectors for the Zendesk full JSON export (with the users export and the error file for tickets over 1 MB) and for Intercom conversations in its API format (with its 500-part limit): cut-short tickets and conversations are reported and never imported half-way unnoticed (tested with fixtures shaped on the vendors’ documentation, not real exports). Reading Intercom directly through its API is pending.

M07.note: Import jobs run in the worker in slices with checkpoints, pause, resume and cancel; every record is keyed by its source ID (scoped to the account it came from), a write with an unknown outcome is looked up before it is repeated, retries are bounded, and a crashed job rerun creates no duplicates (tested with injected faults).

M08.note: Reconciliation per record type (found, imported, skipped, quarantined, failed), fields not imported, the quarantine list with reasons and a CSV download, samples read back from Chatwoot beside the export, a gate that failed checks must be acknowledged at approval, and rollback that keeps live conversations and people still in use (tested, also in browsers). A record retried after a failure lands after its neighbours in Chatwoot, which the sample check reports.

HNV-18-01.note: Choose the brand and the source (tawk.to, Zendesk, Intercom, a Hamnivo package, or another Chatwoot with its access token); files are checked for type and size before sending, and the source is read only (tested in browsers, with accessibility audits right to left). The scope is fixed: conversations with their people and files, or chosen inboxes for Chatwoot.

HNV-18-02.note: Every field in the export is listed with what it becomes, whether it is required and how many records carry it; people are matched only by a verified identity, original times are kept exactly (stored in UTC), and files are shown as imported or links (tested). The mapping is fixed per source: editing it and saving a mapping draft are pending.

HNV-18-03.note: The dry run changes nothing and shows what would be imported, duplicates of earlier imports, records that need review with reasons, and redacted sample conversations (tested). Duplicates are always skipped: what is already in Chatwoot is never overwritten.

HNV-18-04.note: Starting needs a recent sign-in; progress, counts and the last checkpoint show while the worker imports, with pause, resume and cancel at a checkpoint (tested).

HNV-18-05.note: A job that finishes with problems says so, lists each record with its reason, offers them as a CSV and retries only the failed records; missing and quarantined files are listed, never hidden (tested).

HNV-18-06.note: Totals per record type, what was missing from the export, identity and privacy checks, samples beside the export, a cutover checklist and a rollback window until approval (tested, rollback also in Arabic). That live conversations already reach Hamnivo is confirmed by the approver, not measured.

A12.note: Custom roles are built by permission area from the editor's own tenant-wide permissions; anything beyond is refused by the gateway and shown as out of reach. Before saving, the editor shows what is added and removed, what needs two-step verification or a fresh sign-in, and who gains or loses what. Saving needs a fresh sign-in and compares the edited version; a conflict keeps the draft. Built-in roles are read only, and a role is retired only when nobody holds it. Resource scope is chosen per grant, not in the role.

A13.note: Per-workspace OpenID Connect single sign-on through Better Auth's SSO plugin: DNS TXT proof of the email domain (one workspace per verified domain; takeover attempts tested), discovery with HTTPS and public-address checks, the client secret only in the secret broker, optional SSO-only (passwords, sign-ups, resets and passkeys refused), and just-in-time membership with a role within the chooser's reach. An SSO identity joins an existing account only when both addresses are verified. Passkeys (add, sign in, confirm a sensitive action) and signing in again through the provider (prompt=login) are tested in Chromium. SAML and SCIM are not offered.

A17.note: Platform console at /platform for operators named by the server administrator, with platform roles separate from workspace roles and the hamnivo_platform database role: workspaces with metadata only, their plan, trial and usage, service health (API, database, Valkey, queue, connectors), support access, AI stops per workspace, incident banners that every workspace sees, and a hash-chained platform audit log. Platform admins suspend and reactivate workspaces (a suspended workspace is read-only for its staff and its website chat shows offline), change their plan or start a trial, turn public sign-up on or off and manage operator API keys (stored as HMACs) for billing systems. Not built: abuse controls, and stopping AI or switching providers from the platform; AI stops are shown, not operated.

A18.note: Operators ask a workspace for read-only access with a reason, scopes (configuration, the conversation list with status only, audit) and a duration. An owner with two-step verification approves it narrower or shorter, declines it or revokes it; it ends on expiry, revocation or by the operator. Every step and every read is recorded in both the workspace audit log and the platform one, and a banner shows on every Studio page while access is active or waiting.

HNV-22-01.note: Members with role, scope, status and last activity, pending invitations, search, and actions limited to the viewer's reach (checked again by the gateway); inviting works by keyboard alone. Availability is not shown, and inactive or pending people are found by search and their own list rather than a filter.

HNV-22-02.note: Invitations show the address, role, scope, expiry and state; resending replaces the link (the old one stops working) and withdrawing ends it. Accepting needs the invited address, verified; a suspended member can't be invited back.

HNV-22-03.note: Permissions grouped by area with a live preview of what is added and removed, what needs two-step verification or a fresh sign-in, and what lies beyond the editor's reach (refused by the gateway too). Resource scope is chosen when the role is granted.

HNV-22-04.note: Saving sends the edited version, so a role someone else saved meanwhile is never overwritten. Comparing with their version keeps the draft and shows the difference and the people affected before saving again; leaving with unsaved changes asks first.

HNV-22-05.note: Removing first shows the person's open conversations (reassigned in bulk through the inbox), their access and whether they are the last owner. Removal revokes every grant and invitation, ends access on the next request and closes live streams at the next heartbeat; sign-in sessions end when no other workspace keeps the person. Session counts and other modules' pending actions are not listed.

HNV-22-06.note: Actor, time, action, target, outcome, reason and redacted data per event, with filters, a chain integrity check and export (CSV or NDJSON, its own permission and a fresh sign-in, audited). The request ID is in the export rather than the table, and retention is not explained on the page.

HNV-26-01.note: Service states (API, database, Valkey, queue, connectors), queue lag and failing events, connector counts and which platform model keys are set, without any content. Deployment versions, regions and error rates are not shown.

HNV-26-02.note: Workspace ID, state, plan, trial, billing provider, usage this period, workspaces, brands, connectors, AI stops, model providers and support history, read through column grants that leave out content; support access is asked from here. Region is not modelled yet, and owners are reached through the support request, not by address.

HNV-26-03.note: A request names its reason, the areas it needs (configuration, the conversation list with status only, audit) and how long; the workspace sees it at once and nothing is shared until an owner approves. Declined or pending requests leave the operator with metadata only.

HNV-26-04.note: Approved access shows its scope and a countdown to the operator and a banner on every page of the workspace; each read is recorded on both sides. It ends on expiry, revocation or by the operator, after which reads are refused and the console forgets what was read.

HNV-26-06.note: Platform administrators post an incident (title, message for workspaces, severity) that shows as a banner in every workspace until resolved, with both steps in the platform audit log. Pausing a service, scoping the blast radius and a recovery checklist are not built.

D06.note: Tenant HTTPS endpoints with chosen event types, signed per Standard Webhooks (webhook-id, webhook-timestamp, webhook-signature; whsec_ secrets in the secret broker, shown once, both signatures during a rotation overlap). Events come from the outbox: conversations, customer-visible messages, handoffs, orders, payments, refunds, memory deletion receipts and usage alerts, never internal notes. Retries back off exponentially with jitter over about three days (Retry-After respected); 410 or sustained failure turns an endpoint off. The delivery log keeps status, latency and a redacted response excerpt, never secrets; single and filtered replays keep the original webhook-id. Every call goes through the SSRF-safe egress client. The server SDK verifies signatures (official test vectors), timestamps and replays.

X05.note: Every request the server makes at an address a tenant can name goes through one guard (@hamnivo/adapters/net): webhooks, tool calls to remote MCP servers and to custom HTTP tools (and the OpenAPI description they are read from), the websites read for knowledge, identity providers’ discovery documents, migration sources and a tenant’s own model servers. HTTPS only, no credentials in the address, public addresses only: private, loopback, link-local and special-use addresses (one list, the union of what the earlier guards refused) are refused at connect time, on the address actually connected to, so DNS rebinding fails; redirects are never followed; responses have size and time limits. Each workspace can restrict the rest to listed hosts (with wildcards), which MCP servers and model servers follow too; webhook endpoints the list would refuse are shown. Only the server administrator can trust extra origins, and each caller keeps its own setting (EGRESS_TRUSTED_ORIGINS for webhooks and model servers, SSO_TRUSTED_IDP_ORIGINS, and for development TOOLS_EGRESS_ALLOW_PRIVATE and MIGRATION_SOURCE_ALLOW_PRIVATE). One exception: Better Auth’s SSO plugin fetches an identity provider’s token, key and user-info endpoints itself with the global fetch and has no option to replace it. Those addresses are checked with the guard when a connection is saved, and the plugin refuses redirects and private addresses on its own, but its single lookup is not pinned to the connection, so DNS rebinding is not stopped for those three calls.

A08.note: Workspace limits per calendar month (conversations, AI replies, AI tokens) and at any time (knowledge storage, seats, webhook endpoints), metered from usage_entries and enforced with 402 PLAN_LIMIT_REACHED and the numbers (database guards for seats and storage). New workspaces start on the free plan with limits (HAMNIVO_DEFAULT_PLAN=unlimited keeps the old no-limit behaviour for self-hosting). Past the AI limits or the workspace's own token budget, conversations go to people instead. Alerts at 50/80/90/100% are audited and sent as webhook events; each API key has its own rate limit (429 with Retry-After). Per-agent and per-tool budgets are not built.

A15.note: The operator defines plans (seat, volume, storage and endpoint limits, metered prices, trial days, a Stripe price) with the billing command and assigns them there, in the platform console or through the operator API; each workspace keeps a copy as its entitlements, independent of roles and permissions. New workspaces start on the server's default plan (free unless HAMNIVO_DEFAULT_PLAN says otherwise), as a trial when the plan has trial days; a trial falls back to the free plan when it ends.
