Studio shows usage against the limits. Feature entitlements (features switched on per plan) are not built.

A16.note: Invoices drafted per calendar month from the usage ledger (plan price and metered usage), issued, paid or voided, with payment failures and retry dates, audited in the workspace. Billing providers behind a port: free (default), Stripe (Checkout for subscriptions, the Customer Portal, provider invoices, and signed webhooks applied once each and in any order: subscription changes, paid invoices with a receipt email, failed payments with a grace period after which the workspace falls back to the free plan) and WHMCS (a provisioning module that creates, suspends, unsuspends, terminates and re-plans workspaces through the operator API). Workspaces billed by Stripe or WHMCS get no invoice from this server. Tested against a fake Stripe Billing server and with the WHMCS module driving the gateway; not yet against live Stripe or a WHMCS installation.

O04.note: Workspace reports from aggregates only, per date range and time zone, with team and channel filters: conversations per day against the previous period, AI-resolved and handed-off rates, median first response and resolution time, CSAT, handoff reasons, team and channel breakdowns, orders and refunds per currency, AI replies and tokens, and the answer-cache hit rate. Numbers on fewer conversations or responses than ANALYTICS_MIN_GROUP_SIZE are withheld, with complementary suppression; the CSV export follows the same rules. Reopen rate, SLA attainment and cost per resolved case are not built. Also missed chats (no answer within an hour), contact form messages and reopen rate, and a Tickets report: created, closed, open now, median time to close, by priority and by source, with the same withholding of small groups.

HNV-19-01.note: Name, read permissions (none chosen by default), workspace or brand scope and an expiry of 7 to 365 days; a key never gets more than its creator holds, and creating one needs two-step verification and a recent sign-in.

HNV-19-02.note: The key is shown once with a copy button and a storage warning; only an HMAC is stored. Rotation gives a new key with an overlap for the old one; revoking stops it at once.

HNV-19-03.note: HTTPS address checked against the egress policy, event types by group, the signing secret shown once, and a signed test event whose answer (status, outcome, safe error) is shown and marks the endpoint verified.

HNV-19-04.note: Each delivery shows the event ID, attempts, latency, status and a payload preview with people's words and identities hidden (schema version included); replays keep the webhook-id, explain deduplication and are audited.

HNV-19-05.note: Attempt history with the next retry and the final failure reason; failing and turned-off endpoints say why; one delivery or every failed one in a window can be replayed after the endpoint is fixed. No ordering is promised; receivers deduplicate on webhook-id.

HNV-19-06.note: Rate-limited requests answer 429 with Retry-After, the request ID and the key as the quota scope; Studio counts down to when to try again. There are no deprecated API or webhook schema versions yet, so no deprecation notices or migration links.

HNV-23-01.note: Date range and time zone, volume, response times and outcomes with what each number stands on; withheld values say so instead of showing zero, and ranges before reports started recording are disclosed.

HNV-23-02.note: Team and channel filters, visible denominators and a CSV export under the same permissions and withholding. Opening the matching conversations from a number, and language or agent filters, are not built.

HNV-23-03.note: Only the small-sample guard exists (numbers on too few conversations are withheld); quality and fairness regressions from evaluations are not reported yet.

HNV-23-04.note: Plan and billing in Studio settings shows the plan, its trial or grace period, usage against each limit for the current billing month and the invoices; Reports keeps the AI budget and the invoice details. With Stripe, Upgrade opens Checkout and Manage the Customer Portal; with WHMCS, Manage opens the provider's client area. There is no usage forecast.

HNV-23-05.note: Each meter shows when its limit is near or reached and when the period ends; a paused AI says why while conversations continue with people; the workspace can set its own AI budget and alerts. Nothing is deleted at a limit.

HNV-23-06.note: Invoice status, overdue and failed payments, due dates and the past-due notice are shown. With Stripe, a failed payment shows the grace period's end and emails the owners; the payment method and plan are changed in the Customer Portal, and the workspace follows Stripe's events. Plan changes with a chosen effective date are not offered.

W02.note: Four layouts: a floating button, a side panel, inline in an element of the page and the whole page. Each brand chooses one in Studio (widget.configure) and the loader's data-mode overrides it; on screens narrower than 480 px the button and the panel open full screen, sized to the visible area. Tested in the gateway (settings reach new sessions and the launcher, which only allowed websites may read) and in the browser, also at 320 px and 200 % zoom in English and Arabic.

W09.note: Customers upload a file's own bytes into quarantine. The type is read from the bytes, the brand's types, size (up to 10 MB) and count (up to 5) apply, and the scanner (ClamAV in production, the EICAR check in tests) must pass it: any scanner failure, error or timeout refuses the file. Only then does one message carry it to Chatwoot. Downloads come only from the caller's conversation and the customer's view of it, and are scanned again. The widget shows previews and accessible chips with the reason for a refusal. Production without ClamAV offers no files. Mutation-checked.

W17.note: A home before the conversation: the brand's suggested questions in each language, each starting the conversation, and a search of the brand's public knowledge with the assistant's retrieval and the customer audience (internal sources and other brands excluded), limited per session. Results are the brand's own articles, never generated text (tested).

W18.note: A customer signed in by the website's assertion is one principal per brand on every device and continues the same conversations. Anonymous visitors, other customers and the same person on another brand see none of them by any path (list, history, files, stream). Signing in as someone else or out ends the old session's open streams at once. Resuming by an emailed link is not offered (tested, mutation-checked).

W19.note: Website prompts are website automations (G21): page address, referrer, visits, device, country, language, business hours and who is online, all or any, after seconds on the page. The gateway checks what it knows and the loader the rest; at most three a day, a quiet time after a dismissal, one per page view, never over an open chat. The page passes only the automation's id; the chat shows the brand's own words. Staff who may reply can also invite a visitor from Live visitors.

W22.note: Chatwoot CE has no reactions (the adapter reports reactions: false), so a reaction travels as a short customer message quoting the reply (in_reply_to, a stable parent reference) that staff read as such, sent once and never answered by the assistant. Threads (replying to a chosen message) are not offered.

W23.note: Customers delete their own messages within the brand's window (0 to 60 minutes; 0 turns it off). Chatwoot keeps a marker, the journal's stored copies lose their text, and the lane gets one message.redacted whichever path reports it. After the window, or where the authority cannot, the customer is told so. Edits are not offered: Chatwoot CE has no customer edits, so there is no revision history.

W24.note: Shared places and contacts from the authority render as cards (coordinates, phone numbers and addresses validated; links only to a map, tel: and mailto:), and anything unknown falls back to its text. Channel capabilities are one table (CHANNEL_CAPABILITIES): cards render on web chat and travel as their fallback text and link on email, WhatsApp and Telegram; WhatsApp's 24-hour reply window refuses staff replies (CHANNEL_WINDOW_CLOSED), drops automation messages and shows in the composer. Audio, video and polls are not done.

W25.note: Verified customers with a verified address choose transcript and reply-waiting emails, sent through the mailer. Reply emails never carry the reply's text, wait for a delay, skip replies already read and come at most every 30 minutes; transcripts hold only what the customer could see. Every email has a signed one-click unsubscribe link that asks first. Quiet hours are not done.

HNV-05-01.note: Launcher with the real unread count while the chat is closed, also in its accessible name; motion follows reduced-motion settings.

HNV-05-02.note: First visit: greeting, language picker, AI disclosure, suggested questions and help search, and "Talk to a person".

HNV-06-01.note: The draft is kept; attached files show as removable chips with name, size and state, and sending waits for their checks.

HNV-06-02.note: One bubble goes from waiting or sending to Sent; Read only where Chatwoot reports that the team saw it.

HNV-06-03.note: A message that was not sent says why in the customer's language and offers Retry, Edit and Remove.

HNV-06-04.note: Offline banner with the last update and Try again; the message box keeps working and messages wait to be sent once.

HNV-06-05.note: A refused file keeps a tile with the reason: its type (pictures or PDF), the size limit, too many files, possible malware, or a scanner that could not check it.

HNV-06-06.note: While reading back, new replies leave the reading position alone and a button says how many wait.

HNV-07-01.note: On narrow screens the chat opens full screen as one pane; the header wraps, the message box stays reachable and clears the safe area (tested at 320 px and at 200 % zoom).

HNV-07-02.note: A full-screen chat is sized to the visible area (visualViewport), so the on-screen keyboard does not hide the message box; not yet checked on a device with an on-screen keyboard.

G07.note: Tools per brand with an input schema and, for MCP tools, an output schema (both reduced to a portable subset; a result that does not match is refused), a risk class (read, write, money, irreversible), who approves, a required permission, a time limit, an output size limit, an approval expiry and an egress allowlist. Every policy change bumps the revision approvals are bound to and needs tools.manage and a fresh sign-in; money and irreversible tools can never run without approval (tested). A tool can also be a custom HTTP request to a service of the customer’s own: the chosen operations of an OpenAPI 3 description (JSON or YAML, pasted, uploaded or read from an address; references inside the file only, a work limit against files made to be slow to read) or one request written by hand, with its arguments going to the path, the query, a header or a JSON body. Each starts in review with the safest policy, and what the description says about it is shown quoted and never sent to the AI. A call goes through the same gateway, approvals and budgets, only to the service’s host (the tool’s own list and the workspace’s), with the credential read from the secret broker after the arguments make a request that may be sent; a value that would change the shape of the request is refused. A change carries the action’s idempotency key, a refusal by the service is a failure, and an error or silence after sending is never sent again (all tested against a made-up service in the gateway; the screens are unit-tested, with no browser test). Only JSON bodies are supported: forms, files, cookies and sign-ins other than a token or a secret in a header are not.

G08.note: Every tool call goes through one gateway. At the proposal it checks that the conversation is still the AI’s at the run’s epoch, the tool’s status and policy, kill switches, the agent’s grant, the customer’s scope (another customer’s order does not exist for the call) and the budgets. A decision checks who decides: the customer of the conversation, or staff with tools.approve, the tool’s own permission and a fresh sign-in for money and irreversible actions. When someone decides and again right before sending, the tool’s revision, status and kill switches, the agent’s grant, the resource’s revision and the ownership epoch are checked again; a change supersedes the action (tested, mutation-checked).

X02.note: Right before a call is sent, the executor checks again what the approval was bound to: the arguments’ hash, the tool’s revision and status, kill switches, the agent’s grant, the resource’s revision in the customer’s scope and the ownership epoch. Anything changed supersedes the action and nothing is sent (tested: changed order, changed tool, removed grant, kill switch after approval, takeover). Budgets are taken when the action is decided, under the conversation and tenant locks, so they cannot be overrun; turning automatic actions off does not recall one already decided (a kill switch does).

X03.note: Tool calls per run, automatic actions per conversation and per tenant per day, and parallel tool calls (TOOLS_MAX_PARALLEL) have enforced ceilings, and every tool call has a time limit and an output size limit (tested). Missing: cost ceilings, and nesting limits, which belong with multi-agent specialists.

G10.note: When a conversation goes to people, Hamnivo records a packet from its own records: why, the customer’s request and reply language, what the AI tried, actions still pending with their approver and expiry, and the facts it relied on with their source. Staff see it as a private note and in the inbox; it holds no hidden reasoning (tested in the gateway and in a browser).

G11.note: Suites of frozen cases (customer messages and what each tool answers) replay against the draft and the published version with nothing sent; Studio shows what changed, and publishing waits until required suites pass on the exact draft (tested in the gateway and in a browser). Replays use the deterministic mock model, so they show what Hamnivo’s rules do with the draft (tools offered, approvals, budgets, guards), not what the configured model would say. Replaying with the tenant’s own model is not built. Apart from replays, “Test your AI” lets a person try the draft or the live version in a scratch conversation with the agent’s own model connection, its knowledge and its tools’ rules: tools are judged by the live rules and never run, nothing is stored or sent to Chatwoot, every reply goes through the honesty and claim guards, and each turn spends tokens against the plan and budget (tested against a made-up model server in the gateway; the Studio panel is unit-tested, with no browser test). It does not run the brand’s Jev checks.

G13.note: An approval shows the exact action and resource and is bound to the arguments’ SHA-256, the tool’s revision, the resource’s revision and the ownership epoch. Customers approve their own low-risk requests; staff with tools.approve and the tool’s own permission approve the rest, after a fresh sign-in for money and irreversible actions; a customer can never approve a staff action. Approvals expire, any change supersedes them, and decided approvals are append-only (tested, mutation-checked).

G14.note: A change counts as done only with a succeeded receipt in the operation ledger. A lost answer leaves the outcome unknown: the tool’s own records settle it, it is never sent again, and staff can ask for a check or record the outcome by hand. An AI reply that says something was done without a receipt is regenerated with a correction, then goes to people (tested, mutation-checked).

G15.note: Only read and write tools whose policy allows it, granted with autopilot to the agent, run without approval, within per-run, per-conversation and per-tenant daily budgets and a tenant switch; money and irreversible tools never do. A call proposed after reading another system’s data, or with the budget spent, asks for approval, and kill switches stop tools at once (tested).

W16.note: Approval cards show the exact change, its effects, who approves and when the request expires; Approve and Decline work by keyboard, right to left at phone width, with the card’s hash; a request that needs the customer to sign in tells the website. Result cards come only from receipts (browser-tested). Task forms are not built.

D10.note: Remote MCP servers over Streamable HTTP only, on MCP 2025-11-25, 2025-06-18 or 2025-03-26 (others are refused), all through the egress guard; documented in the adapters README. A server is signed in to with a pasted token or with OAuth as the MCP authorization spec describes (discovery, PKCE, a client Hamnivo registers or a client ID a person enters, the resource indicator, renewal before the access ends), using the SDK’s own client helpers; tokens, refresh tokens and client registrations are kept in the secret broker and only the last characters of a pasted token are ever shown. A server can be renamed, moved (its tools go back to review and a credential never follows to another site), given a new token, turned off or removed. What a server lists besides tools (resources and prompts) is shown quoted in Studio; agents with the built-in “Read a resource” tool read only the resources a person allowed, in pieces, and what they propose after reading waits for a person. A catalog of thirteen remote servers that vendors run themselves comes with the vendor page that names each address and the day it was read. Every new or changed tool waits in review before it can be granted or called, and gets Hamnivo’s own description and its own host allowlist (tested). Hamnivo also runs an MCP server of its own at /mcp (read-only tools, an API key that holds mcp.read, a rate limit, every call in the audit log). Custom HTTP tools turn the operations of an OpenAPI 3 description, or one request written by hand, into tools of the same kind: see G07. Tests use made-up MCP and authorization servers on the loopback interface and none talks to a third-party server; the catalog’s addresses are not called.

HNV-11-03.note: The agent editor grants tools, each shown with what it can do and who approves; a grant is part of a versioned draft and the test room shows the cases it changes (browser-tested). Stopping a tool takes effect at once, also for approvals already given (tested in the gateway); removing a grant takes effect with the next published version and cancels open requests for it when they are decided or sent.

HNV-11-04.note: The test room replays a suite against the draft and the published version, labelled “Test only: nothing was sent”, with each version’s replies, the actions and decisions per case and what changed; every run starts from the frozen cases (browser-tested). Replies come from the deterministic mock model (see G11).

HNV-11-05.note: Publishing is refused while a required suite has not passed on the exact draft, or a granted tool is waiting for review or belongs to another brand. The dialog names the check and what to do, the live version stays as it was, and after the suite is run again the draft publishes (browser-tested).

HNV-13-01.note: Lookups run with a time limit, their results are contained, and a failure reaches the customer in safe words without credentials; stopping the run cancels a call in flight (tested in the gateway). The inbox lists each lookup with its state. Missing: a browser test of a lookup while it runs.

HNV-13-02.note: Customers and staff see the exact target, values, effects, approver and expiry and approve exactly that or decline (browser-tested); a changed request needs a new approval (tested in the gateway). Missing: editing a proposal before approving (today: decline and ask again).

HNV-13-03.note: An expired or changed request can no longer be approved: the card and the inbox say why in words, and a new request is a new card with a new hash (tested in the gateway). Missing: highlighting the fields that changed, and a browser test.

HNV-13-04.note: A refused action carries a reason safe to show (turned off, stopped, limit reached, not found for this customer…); the AI tells the customer it could not do it and that a person can help, and staff see the reason in the inbox and the audit log (tested in the gateway). Missing: offering an allowed alternative, a link to the audit entry, and a browser test.

HNV-13-05.note: A write whose answer was lost shows as not confirmed, with its action reference; it is never sent again, the tool’s records settle it, and staff can ask for a check or record the outcome by hand (tested in the gateway). Missing: a browser test of these inbox controls.

J03.note: Evidence: before the model sees retrieved passages, the passage relevance check asks Jev three questions per passage, one request each with only the question and that passage: is it about the question, does it answer it, does it carry instructions for the assistant. Code decides, first match wins: instructions drop it, off-topic drops it, an answer keeps it, no answer drops it; an unsure passage is kept. Live drops them and records which (document ids and reasons, no text); shadow, every brand's start, records only; a passage Jev could not judge is kept. Verified live on 2026-10-02 with jev-1.13.0: a passage carrying instructions and an off-topic one were left out and the returns policy kept (247 ms for three passages in parallel). No thresholds were evaluated yet: brands set them per language. Skill ranking is not built.

A01.note: A guided setup opens after a workspace is created and from Home: workspace, brand and website, the chat engine (connected by itself), an AI key with a test, a test chat, install with a guide per website platform, and the team. Every step can be skipped, and what was done or skipped is kept at the gateway, so the owner resumes where they stopped. Home’s checklist now puts the brand first, adds the AI key, and does not count an agent that answers with the offline practice model. Knowledge, a handoff team and publishing the agent are not steps of the guide yet (Home’s list covers publishing), and Studio cannot check that the install code is on the website. Screens are tested as rendered HTML and the logic in unit tests; there is no browser journey for it.

A05.note: Owners set each brand’s hours in Studio: a time zone, a week of opening spans (several on one day, such as a lunch break), quick starts, and whole days closed such as public holidays. The times are checked before saving and the hours can be removed, after which the chat never claims a person is available. Clock changes are handled by the domain rules. The page is tested as rendered HTML and its logic in unit tests; there is no browser journey for it.

HNV-01-01.note: A new workspace opens the guided setup. It has seven skippable steps, not three, and shows no region or data location.

HNV-01-02.note: Brand name and website, then the install step. Website is the only channel, so there is no choice of channel.

HNV-01-03.note: The install code with a copy confirmation, the allowed websites, readable steps and a guide for the website platform. There is no connection check: Studio cannot see the website, and the step says so and how to check by hand.

HNV-01-05.note: The step list shows what is done, skipped or still to do; leaving keeps all of it; Home links back in and the guide opens at the first step still open. Any step can be skipped.

HNV-04-01.note: A live picture of the chat (any of the four languages, team online or away), a contrast check with a darker suggestion to apply, reset to the saved look. Changes save straight to the chat (there is no draft), and there is no mobile viewport or launcher placement here.

HNV-04-02.note: The greeting and the offline message in four languages (English first), and the business hours on their own page. No journey preview and no identity label settings.

HNV-04-04.note: An invalid colour, address or text is explained next to its field and in a linked error summary, and what was typed is kept. The gateway checks again and its reasons are shown the same way.

W26.note: Up to six questions per brand in four languages (name, email, phone, question, team, short text, list), checked by the gateway when the chat starts. The name names the customer; a typed email and phone become contact attributes and are never the customer's verified address; a team answer sets the conversation's team, which routing then leaves alone; staff get every answer in a private note; the question becomes the first message. Customers the website signed in may skip it.

W27.note: Off, every visitor, or connections from the EU, EEA and UK (unknown countries are asked too); the country is read per request and never stored. Never pre-ticked; the gateway refuses a chat without agreement to the current words, and new words ask again. Agreements are append-only, with the words' version and the time.

W28.note: The chat on its own page at /c/<widget>, off by default; a session from the link is allowed only while the brand keeps it on, and turning it off ends those sessions at their next renewal. Caddy serves the page unframable and with noindex. Studio shows the link, a QR code (SVG, downloadable) and the install code.

H19.note: A ticket is a conversation with a tenant-wide number (ADR 0010): Open, Pending (snoozed until the customer writes) or Closed (resolved), with Chatwoot's priority set as the staff member and taken over when changed in Chatwoot. From the contact form or by staff; a Tickets queue with state and priority filters; every change audited and fenced by the ownership epoch. The queue orders by activity, not priority. The Chatwoot contract cases run against the fake here; the real run is left to CI.

G21.note: A When / If / Then form rather than a canvas: one event, up to 10 conditions (all or any) and up to 5 actions, from templates, with a Try it panel that uses the same evaluator as the worker. Drafts, immutable published versions, restore, a 90-day run log. Chat rules run from the outbox once per conversation and event; messages never while the AI has the chat, at most five a day. Partial: no branches or loops, and no external tool steps.

HNV-28-01.note: Typed event and conditions with readable summaries and a draft state; no branches.

HNV-28-03.note: Try it evaluates a sample visitor or chat with the worker's own evaluator and has no side effects.

HNV-28-04.note: Loops cannot start: automation messages never trigger rules, and a rule acts once per conversation and event. No hooks or plugins.

HNV-28-05.note: Publishing keeps an immutable version and checks the rule; restore copies a version into the draft. No staged rollout or diff view.

H20.note: Block from a chat or from Live visitors with a required reason and 24 hours, 7 days, 30 days or until lifted; never an IP address: the customer, their browser key and a signed-in account. The widget says only that chat isn't available; reading, help, privacy choices, sign-in and the tracking notice stay open. Blocking again keeps one block; blocks are lifted, not deleted, audited, and purged 90 days after they end. Senders on email, WhatsApp and Telegram can be blocked too (one address on one channel): their messages are kept, but nothing answers or follows (no AI, ticket, team or automations), and each conversation is closed with a private note; they are never told.

HNV-31-01.note: Required reason, four durations, Also close this chat; Blocked list with Unblock and a confirm step; axe in English and Arabic.

D13.note: Connect the brand's mailbox from Settings → Channels (IMAP and SMTP, provider presets with app-password links): Chatwoot creates the email inbox, checks the sign-in and keeps the passwords; Hamnivo stores none, never keeps the request for replays, and shows Chatwoot's refusal next to the field. Every email conversation Chatwoot creates is adopted (ADR 0013) and becomes a ticket (source email); replies thread through Chatwoot's In-Reply-To. AI answers only where the owner turned it on; no-reply and mailer-daemon senders reach people but get no automatic answer. A mailbox Chatwoot can no longer sign in to shows Needs attention until a new password works. Tested end to end against the fake (15 cases) and in Studio. The ticket number is not in the email subject: Chatwoot's API cannot change it.

D14.note: Connect a WhatsApp Business number (Meta Cloud API) or a Telegram bot from Settings → Channels: Chatwoot checks the token with Meta or Telegram and keeps it; Hamnivo stores none. For WhatsApp, Studio shows the callback URL on Chatwoot's public host and Chatwoot's verify token for Meta's webhook set-up. Their conversations are adopted like email (ADR 0013), with the AI off until the owner turns it on, and Telegram is its own channel in the inbox. Tested end to end against the fake; creating WhatsApp and Telegram inboxes against a real Chatwoot needs Meta and Telegram, so the contract suite runs those cases on the fake only. Past the 24-hour window, staff send Meta-approved templates from the composer: Chatwoot's synced list is read live, values are checked and the rendered text is what the customer reads; sent once through the message ledger. Templates with a media header and one-time-code templates are not sent from Hamnivo.
